rationale: Since (ib+xrd)/ME and −ib/ME differ only by xrd/ME, the product of their ranks mechanically selects high R&D-to-market firms, making this a thinly disguised rediscovery of the well-published R&D-to-market anomaly (Chan-Lakonishok-Sougiannis) rather than a new accounting-distortion interaction, and the second leg also loads on loss firms.

The conditional structure is copied verbatim from the archive's strongest signal with only the valuation lens swapped (ib/ME → EBITDA/EV), which is a robustness check rather than a substantively different mechanism, and the archive's IntangibleBurdenEVYield already showed the EBITDA/EV lens delivers positive FMB slopes with negative FF5 alpha.

Rescaling the sales-response leg by assets-plus-R&D-capital is a legitimate diagnostic fix for the earlier signal's tiny-denominator and 3.8% coverage problem, though the second leg is close to asset-scaled sales growth (a documented negative predictor) and the closely related CommercializingKnowledgeValue already produced a significantly negative FF5 alpha, so the positive sign is not well secured.

Adding R&D-intensity stability is a genuinely new conditioning dimension, but the switch to a pure triple-rank product reverts to the mechanical zeroing-out of non-R&D value firms that the archive's additive design was built to avoid, and the 5-year VOL requirement will further thin coverage.

Conditioning book-to-market on internally generated versus acquired intangible composition is an economically coherent and not-yet-tested distinction in this archive, though the difference term will be dominated by R&D/assets and the multiplicative form may leave the extreme deciles sparsely populated since high-B/M firms rarely carry heavy R&D.

Adding a fundamental-deterioration leg is a substantive rather than cosmetic response to AcquisitionIntangibleOverpayRisk's sign disagreement between FMB and FF5 alpha, but declining sales-to-assets is largely the asset-growth anomaly in disguise, so a negative result may reflect known effects rather than the goodwill-overpayment channel.
